The prohibition applies only to deliberate listening, not merely hearing. Thus, if a man passes people engaged in forbidden speech, he is not obliged to stop his ears, but he may not deliberately listen without a need. Likewise, the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—did not instruct Ibn ʿUmar to stop his ears when he heard a shepherd’s flute, because he was merely hearing it, not deliberately listening.

The question posed by this questioner and others—“Is it lawful or unlawful?”—is ambiguously worded and obscures the issue. The ruling becomes so confused that many muftis cannot formulate a precise answer. This is because listening, like other actions, may be considered from two perspectives:

The first concerns whether it is prohibited or not—whether it may be practised like other activities that people enjoy, even if they involve some amusement and play, such as listening at weddings and similar occasions. People engage in these activities for pleasure and amusement, not as worship or to draw closer to Allah.

The second is to engage in it as a religious observance and an act of worship, to reform hearts, make the servants’ love for their Lord pure and undivided, cleanse their souls and purify their hearts

A distinction must therefore be drawn between listening practised by those seeking nearness to Allah and listening practised for amusement; between listening at weddings, celebrations, and similar customary occasions, and listening intended to reform hearts and draw closer to the Lord of the heavens. Concerning the latter, the questions are:

Is it an act of devotion and obedience? Is it a path to Allah? Can they do without it, given that it softens their hearts, stirs their ardent love for their Beloved, purifies their souls, removes hardness from their hearts, and serves other such purposes sought through listening? Christians likewise practise this kind of listening in their churches as worship and obedience, not as amusement and play.

Once this is understood, the real question is:

Is it permissible for the shaykh to make these practices—which are either prohibited, disliked, or permissible—into acts of devotion, worship, and obedience, and a path to Allah through which he calls people to Allah, leads sinners to repentance, directs those who have gone astray, and guides the misguided?

It is well known that religion has “two foundations”: nothing belongs to religion except what Allah has prescribed, and nothing is forbidden except what Allah has forbidden. Allah Most High has reproached the polytheists for forbidding what He has not forbidden and instituting a religion for which He has given no permission.

And if a scholar were asked about someone running between two mountains, “Is he permitted to do that?” he would answer, “Yes.” But if he were told, “He does so as an act of worship, like making the passage between al-Safā and al-Marwah,” he would say, “Doing this as worship is forbidden and reprehensible. The person doing it must be called upon to repent; if he does not repent, he is to be put to death.”

Likewise, if he were asked about leaving the head uncovered and wearing a waist-wrapper and an upper-body wrap, he would rule that this is permissible. But if he were told, “He does so as a form of ihrām (ritual consecration), as a pilgrim does,” he would say, “This is forbidden and reprehensible.”

If he were asked about someone standing in the sun, he would say, “This is permissible.” But if he were told, “He does so as an act of worship,” he would say, “This is reprehensible,” as al-Bukhārī narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās—may Allah be pleased with them both:

“Allah’s Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, saw a man standing in the sun and asked, ‘Who is this?’ They said, ‘This is Abū Isrā’īl. He intends to stand in the sun without sitting down, seeking shade, or speaking.’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘Tell him to speak, sit down, seek shade, and complete his fast.’”

Had he done this for his own comfort or some permissible purpose, he would not have been forbidden to do it. But because he did it as an act of worship, he was forbidden to do so. Similarly, if a man entered his house from the back, that would not be forbidden to him. But if he did so as an act of worship, as people used to do in the pre-Islamic period:

when one of them entered ihrām, he would not go under a roof—they were forbidden to do this, as the Most High says:

“Righteousness is not in entering houses from the back. Rather, righteousness is in fearing Allah. So enter houses through their doors.”

He, glorified be He, thus made clear that this is not righteousness, even though it is not itself forbidden. Whoever does it as an act of righteousness and a means of drawing near to Allah is therefore disobedient, blameworthy, and an innovator. Religious innovation is dearer to Iblīs than sin, because the sinner knows that he is sinning and so repents, whereas the innovator imagines that what he is doing is an act of obedience and therefore does not repent.

Likewise, someone who attends gatherings for listening to poetry for amusement and entertainment does not count this among his righteous deeds or hope to be rewarded for it. But someone who does so as a path to Allah Most High makes it part of his religion. If someone forbids him to do it, he regards that person as forbidding his religion, and believes that abandoning it would cut him off from Allah and deprive him of his portion from Allah Most High.

Such people are misguided by agreement of the Muslim scholars. None of the imams of the Muslims says that adopting this as a religious practice and a path to Allah Most High is permissible. Rather, whoever makes this a religious practice and a path to Allah Most High is misguided, fabricates falsehood, and opposes the consensus of the Muslims. Anyone who considers only the outward form of an action and pronounces upon it, without considering how the person performs it and what he intends, is ignorant and speaks about religion without knowledge.

The question about such a matter should therefore be put as follows:

“Is what these people do a path to Allah Most High, a means of drawing near to Him, and an act of obedience that Allah and His Messenger love, or not? Will they be rewarded for it or not? If this is not a means of drawing near to Allah, an act of obedience to Him, or worship of Him, yet they do it as a means of drawing near to Him

and as an act of obedience and worship and a path to Allah Most High, is it permissible for them to hold this belief and perform this practice on that basis?”

When the question is put this way, no scholar who follows the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—can say that this is a means of drawing near to Allah, an act of obedience, a form of worship, or part of Allah’s way and the path by which these people call others to Him. Nor can he say that it is something Allah Most High has commanded His servants to do, whether as an obligation or as a recommendation. Whatever is neither obligatory nor recommended is not praiseworthy, a good deed, an act of obedience, or worship, by agreement of the Muslims. Whoever does something neither obligatory nor recommended, treating it as belonging to either category, is a misguided innovator. Performing it on this basis is undoubtedly forbidden.

This applies especially to the many people who adopt this innovated practice of listening as a spiritual path and prefer it to listening to the Quran in terms of ecstasy and spiritual experience. They may even believe it to be superior. Thus, you find them listening to the Quran with heedless hearts, idle talk, restless movements, and raised voices. Their hearts do not turn towards it, nor do their souls find comfort in it. But when they hear “whistling” and “clapping,” their hearts listen intently, the beloved is united with the lover, voices grow hushed, and movements cease. There is no coughing, sneezing, clamour, or shouting.

If they recite or hear anything of the Quran, they do so reluctantly, as though subjected to forced labour, just as a person does not listen to something for which he has no need

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

I have previously written about “unveilings and visions,” explaining that they fall into “three categories,” both outwardly and inwardly. Likewise, “hearing, being addressed, and conversations” fall into three categories, inwardly and outwardly.

The “listener” may hear the actual sound itself, whether it is the speaker’s vocal speech or something other than his speech, just as one sees the speaker himself.

Or he may hear the sound’s echo and reverberation, just as he sees the speaker’s image in water or a mirror. Such seeing and hearing are qualified, as when one says, “I saw him in the mirror.” Hearing, however, encompasses both forms.

Or a representation may be presented to him—meaning the speaker’s words—in audible sounds, just as the speaker may be represented to him in a form that he sees. For example, the speaker may tap with his hand, pluck strings with his hand, or produce sounds separate from himself through which he conveys his intended meaning.

translated_text:
And likewise inwardly:

A person may hear, in sleep or while awake, the speaker’s actual words—for example, those of angels—just as he sees with his heart the very thing unveiled to him in sleep or wakefulness. Or he may hear a representation of the speaker’s words within himself, just as he sees a representation of the speaker within himself, like a dream whose interpretation is the very thing seen. Or meanings may be represented to him as audible speech requiring interpretation, just as actual things may be represented to him as visible figures requiring interpretation. This is the case with most of what is seen and heard in dreams: it requires interpretation and resembles metaphor and illustrative parables. Such is the matter. And Allah knows best.

Section

On Existence in Wakefulness and Sleep

Seeing things with the eye takes two forms:

The first is the eye’s seeing an object without an intermediary. This is seeing in the unqualified sense, such as seeing the sun and the moon. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“You will see your Lord just as you see the sun and the moon.”

People have differed over whether vision consists in the object seen being imprinted upon the eye, results from the reflection of visual rays, or involves neither. These are well-known positions.

The second is seeing an image, as when looking into water, a mirror, or the like. This is a qualified form of seeing. Thus, the jurists have said that if someone swears, “I shall not see Zayd,” then sees his image in water or a mirror, he has not broken his oath, because this is not what is understood by seeing without qualification. This is to sight what hearing an echo is to hearing.

When someone wishes to see the people and animals passing behind him, he looks into a mirror facing him, and it reveals to him what is actually behind him. In this kind of vision, he may see reality clearly, or reality may appear to him in a representation that requires verification, just as Gabriel appeared in human form. Likewise, the heart has the capacity to see, for its sight is true sight, and its blindness is true blindness. As Allah Most High says:

“For it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

At times, the heart sees the thing itself when it is unveiled to it; at other times, it sees the thing represented within itself, serving as its mirror, while also being that which sees. This may occur either in wakefulness or in sleep, as when a man sees something in a dream and then encounters that very thing while awake, without any change.

The heart also has a “third state,” just as the eye has a way of seeing in sleep. This is what most people experience: seeing a dream that presents an illustrative likeness of reality. A person cannot fully grasp the vision of reality itself, either directly or through the mirror of his heart. What is seen in this manner—in this state and in the preceding one—exists within a person’s heart and soul, even though it is a likeness of reality and a means of apprehending it.

What is seen in the first manner, however, is the very thing that exists externally, not something seen within the heart. Some philosophizing laypeople claim that the speech the prophets hear and the angels they see exist only within their hearts. Such is the extent of their knowledge, for that is the furthest limit of what they have experienced and witnessed among their fellow human beings, so they suppose that nothing lies beyond it. Others may oppose them, imagining that what is heard and seen cannot exist within a person, but must all come from outside. Both views are mistaken.

Rather, some of it exists within a person, such as what one sees and hears in sleep, whether an image that admits of no interpretation or one that does.

It is reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“I have only forbidden two foolish, sinful sounds: the sound of frivolity, play, and Satan’s flutes; and the sound of slapping cheeks or tearing garments at the neckline and uttering the cries of the days of ignorance.”

Examples include their cries: “Oh, my sorrow! Oh, my anguish! Oh, my helper!”

Groups of people endowed with spiritual unveiling have been shown the presence of devils at gatherings of devotional listening conducted in the manner of the days of ignorance, with whistling and clapping. They have also been shown how Satan assails those present until they enter a satanic ecstasy, to the point that some begin dancing above the heads of those attending. One of the shaykhs endowed with such unveiling saw that his devil had lifted him up and was making him dance. When he shouted at his devil, it fled, and the man fell.

These matters have secrets and underlying realities witnessed only by those endowed with insight born of faith and spiritual witnessing grounded in certainty. Yet whoever follows what the revealed Law has brought and turns away from the path of those who introduce religious innovations has attained guidance and the good of this world and the Hereafter, even if he does not understand the underlying realities of these matters. He is like someone who takes the road to Mecca, following a guide who knows the way: he reaches his destination and finds provisions and water in their proper places, even if he does not know how this comes about or what brings it about. translated_text:
who shows the way strays from the path. He either perishes or suffers hardship for a time before returning to the path. The “guide who shows the way” is the Messenger whom Allah sent to mankind as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner, calling to Allah by His permission, a shining lamp, and a guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth.

The effects of Satan manifest themselves among those who engage in devotional listening in the manner of the days of ignorance: foaming and frothing at the mouth, dreadful screams, and other things resembling the condition of those whom Satan afflicts with seizures. Thus, depending on the sound, they find within themselves a surge of the impulses Satan desires: ecstasy in blameworthy passion; anger and aggression against someone they wrong; or slapping themselves, tearing their clothes, and crying out like someone stricken with grief and bereft. These and other satanic effects also afflict those who gather to drink wine when they become intoxicated. Intoxication through captivating sounds may become like intoxication through intoxicating drinks: it turns them away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, and deprives their hearts of the sweetness of the Quran, of understanding its meanings, and of following it. They thus come to resemble those who purchase distracting tales to lead others astray from Allah’s path. It also sows enmity and hatred among them, until they kill one another through their corrupt, satanic states, just as someone who casts the evil eye may kill the person it strikes.

For this reason, some scholars have stated that such people are liable to retaliation and blood money

and retributive punishment, if it is established that the victims were killed through corrupt, satanic states. For they are wrongdoers who merely exult in fulfilling their forbidden desires, just as oppressors vested with power exult.

Of this kind are the protectors of unbelievers, innovators, and wrongdoers. They may possess asceticism, devotion, and strength of resolve, as may polytheists and the People of the Book, and as did the Khārijites who departed from Islam, concerning whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“One of you would consider his prayer insignificant beside theirs, his fasting beside theirs, and his recitation beside theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not go beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Alongside this, they may possess inward states, just as they may possess outward power, for inward authority has the same significance as outward authority. Yet none can be among Allah’s allies except those who believe and are mindful of Him. Whatever they have done to assist oppression deserves punishment proportionate to their sin.

Possessing power and influence, inwardly or outwardly, does not necessarily entail being an ally of Allah Most High. Rather, an ally of Allah may possess power and authority, or he may be oppressed until Allah grants him victory; he may also be granted dominion until Allah exacts vengeance upon him. Thus, the inward protectors of the Tatars are of the same kind as the outward Tatars. The former occupy the same position among worshippers as the latter do among soldiers.

As for victory, Allah Most High may at times grant the unbelievers victory over the believers, just as He grants the believers victory over the unbelievers. Such was the case with the Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and their enemies. Yet the ultimate outcome belongs to those who are mindful of Allah, for Allah says:

“Indeed, We will support Our messengers and those who believe during the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth.”

When the Muslims are weak and their enemies have the upper hand over them, this is because of their sins and misdeeds: either their neglect of their inward and outward obligations, or their transgression of the limits, inwardly and outwardly.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met—it was Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned.”

And He Most High says:

“Why, when a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How has this come about?’ Say, ‘It is from your own selves.’”

And He Most High says:

“Allah will surely support those who support His cause. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Almighty.”

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of all affairs.”

He was asked about women who wear large turbans and will neither see Paradise nor smell its fragrance, given that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, is reported to have said:

“Whoever says, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ will enter Paradise.”

He answered:

It is established in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“There are two groups among the people of Hell from my community whom I have not yet seen: women who are clothed yet naked, turning aside and drawing others aside, with something resembling the humps of Bactrian camels upon their heads. They will neither enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance. And men carrying whips like cattle’s tails, with which they beat Allah’s servants.”

Anyone who claims that this hadith is not authentic because of the stern warning it contains is ignorant and has strayed from the revealed law. He deserves punishment that will deter him and other ignorant people like him who challenge authentic hadiths from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. There are many authentic hadiths containing warnings of punishment, such as his saying:

“Whoever kills

a person protected by a covenant without lawful cause will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, although its fragrance can be detected from a distance of forty years’ journey.”

Likewise, his saying recorded in the Sahīh:

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.”

He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, a man likes his clothes and shoes to look fine. Is that arrogance?”

He replied, “No. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and despising people.”

“Rejecting the truth” means denying it, and “despising people” means holding them in contempt and looking down on them.

Likewise, his saying in an authentic hadith:

“There are three whom Allah will neither speak to nor purify on the Day of Resurrection, and theirs will be a painful punishment: an elderly adulterer, a lying king, and an arrogant poor man.”

The Quran contains many verses warning of punishment, such as His saying:

“Indeed, those who unjustly consume the wealth of orphans are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing Fire.”

Likewise, His saying:

“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, but only through trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.”

“And whoever does that in aggression and injustice—We will cast him into a Fire. And that is easy for Allah.”

And His saying concerning the prescribed shares of inheritance:

“These are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.”

“And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein forever, and he will have a humiliating punishment.”

And Muslims are agreed on this: the Quran and Sunnah contain threats of punishment for those who commit major sins. However, Allah has made clear in His Book and His Messenger’s Sunnah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—that these threats do not apply to those who repent. He says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

That is, for those who repent. In another verse, He says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

This concerns those who have not repented. Associating partners with Allah is not forgiven, while anything less than that He forgives if He wills, or punishes if He wills.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“No fatigue, illness, worry, distress, sorrow, or harm befalls a believer—even the prick of a thorn—without Allah thereby expiating some of his sins.”

Thus, when His saying, “Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it,” was revealed, Abū Bakr said, “O Messenger of Allah, this is a crushing blow! Which of us has not done evil?”

He replied, “O Abū Bakr, do you not grow weary? Do you not grieve? Do you not suffer hardship? That is part of the recompense you receive.”

Through worldly afflictions, Allah expiates those sins of a believer that such afflictions can expiate. The same applies to the good deeds he performs. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, good deeds do away with evil deeds.”

He was asked:

“Is there a defining criterion by which the major sins mentioned in the Quran and hadith can be recognized? Is the view that they number seven or seventeen correct? Or the view that they are those on which the revealed laws agree—that is, on their prohibition? Or that they are those that bar the way to knowledge of Allah? Or those that destroy property and lives? Or that they are called major only in comparison and relation to lesser sins? Or that they cannot be identified at all and have been left unspecified, like the Night of Decree? Or, as some report, that their number is closer to ninety? Or that everything Allah has forbidden is a major sin? Or that they are sins carrying a prescribed punishment, or those for which the Fire has been threatened?”

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

The soundest view on this question is the one transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās and cited by Abū ‘Ubayd, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others: a minor sin is one that does not incur either of the two penalties—the penalty in this world and the penalty in the Hereafter.

This is the meaning of the statement, “A sin for which there is no prescribed punishment in this world.” It is also the meaning of the statement, “Every sin accompanied by a curse, wrath, or the Fire is a major sin.”

Among the punishments people are commanded to administer, a distinction is drawn between prescribed penalties—amputation, execution, and one hundred or eighty lashes—and punishments whose extent is not prescribed, namely “discretionary punishments.” Likewise, among the punishments with which Allah chastises His servants—rather than commanding people to administer them—a distinction is drawn between specified punishments, such as wrath, a curse, and the Fire, and punishments described only in general terms.

This “criterion” is free of the objections raised against the others, for it encompasses everything established by the revealed texts as a major sin: associating partners with Allah, murder, unlawful sexual intercourse, sorcery, accusing chaste, unsuspecting believing women of adultery, and other major sins carrying prescribed legal penalties. It also encompasses fleeing the battlefield, devouring an orphan’s wealth, taking usury, mistreating one’s parents, knowingly swearing a false oath, and giving false testimony. These sins and others like them carry specific threats, as Allah says concerning fleeing the battlefield:

“And whoever turns his back on them that day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another group—has incurred Allah’s wrath. His refuge is Hell—what an evil destination!”

And He says:

“Indeed, those who unjustly consume the wealth of orphans are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing Fire.”

Rather, in matters of divine promise and warning, a believer in the unqualified sense—one deserving to enter Paradise without punishment—is someone who fulfils the obligations and avoids what is forbidden. These are the people meant when believers are mentioned without qualification. Whoever commits these major sins is not among these believers, since he exposes himself to punishment for the major sin he has committed. This is what is meant by those who say that the intent is to deny the reality of faith or its completeness. They do not mean the recommended degree of completeness, for falling short of that does not warrant blame or a warning of punishment. Jurists say that ritual bathing has two forms: complete and sufficient. Yet someone who opts for the sufficient form rather than the complete form is not blameworthy. Thus, anyone who understands “denying the completeness of faith” as denying its recommended completeness is mistaken. This resembles the position of the Murji’ah. Rather, what is denied is its obligatory completeness.

This principle applies consistently to everything else that Allah and His Messenger have negated. For example, Allah says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them,”

continuing to His words:

“Those are the believers in truth.”

Likewise, the transmitted hadith states:

“There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy, and no religion in one who does not honour his covenant.”

Such wording therefore indicates that whoever does this has neglected an obligation without which the obligatory degree of faith is incomplete, even though he retains some faith. Faith consists of parts and varies in degree. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will come out of the Fire.”

And (the point here is that denying someone faith or Paradise, or denying that he is among the believers, can only be on account of a major sin. Minor sins alone do not deprive their perpetrator of this designation and status. Thus, we know that this denial is not due to neglecting something recommended or committing a minor sin, but rather to committing a major sin.

We have said that this criterion is preferable to all the other criteria mentioned for several reasons.

First: it is transmitted from the early generations, unlike those other criteria. They are not known to have been stated by any of the Companions, the Successors, or the imams. Rather, they were proposed, without any evidence from revelation, by some who discussed matters of speculative theology or Sufism.

As for those of the early generations who said that they are closer to seventy than to seven, this does not contradict what we have stated. We shall discuss them one by one, Allah willing.

Second: Allah says:

“If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden to commit, We will expiate your misdeeds and admit you to a place of honor.”

He has thus promised those who avoid major sins that their misdeeds will be expiated and that they will receive what He has graciously promised. Anyone threatened with Allah’s wrath, His curse, the Fire, exclusion from Paradise, or anything implying these consequences falls outside this promise and therefore cannot be among those who avoid major sins. Likewise, someone who deserves a prescribed legal punishment has not had his misdeeds expiated through avoiding major sins. Were that so, he would have no sin for which he deserved punishment, whereas someone who deserves a prescribed legal punishment has committed a sin for which he deserves to be punished.

Third: This criterion rests on what Allah and His Messenger have said concerning sins. It is therefore a definition derived from the words of the Lawgiver. The other criteria are not derived from the words of Allah and His Messenger; rather, they express their proponents’ personal opinions and intuitions, without evidence from revelation. Relying on opinion and intuition without evidence from revelation is not permissible.

Fourth: This criterion makes it possible to distinguish major sins from minor sins, whereas those other criteria do not. There is no evidence to support those characteristics, for the distinction between matters on which the revealed laws agree and those on which they differ cannot be known unless it is possible for someone to have an accurate knowledge of those laws; and that is not known to us.

Fifth: Those views are unsound. The view that major sins are those whose prohibition is agreed upon by all revealed laws, excluding matters on which they differ, implies that taking a single grain from an orphan’s property, or obtaining it through theft or breach of trust, telling a single lie, committing certain inconspicuous wrongs, and similar acts are major sins. It also implies that fleeing the battlefield is not a major sin, since jihad was not obligatory under every revealed law. Likewise, it implies that marrying women forbidden through milk kinship, marriage ties, or other grounds is not a major sin, because the revealed laws did not agree on this prohibition. The same applies to retaining one’s wife after divorcing her three times and having intercourse with her thereafter, while believing this to be forbidden.

Likewise, the view that major sins are those that block the path to knowledge or cause the loss of lives and property implies that even a little anger or breach of trust is a major sin, whereas mistreating one’s parents, severing kinship ties, drinking wine, eating carrion or pork, slandering chaste, unsuspecting believing women, and similar acts are not major sins.

He—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

Which is a greater sin before Allah: drinking wine or committing sexual indecency? Or are they equal?

What are the major sins concerning which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

“If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will expiate your lesser sins and admit you to a place of honour”?

What, then, are these major sins, and what are the lesser sins?

He—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

All praise is due to Allah. “Major sins” are those for which a punishment is prescribed in this world or in the Hereafter. These include unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, and falsely accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse, which carry prescribed legal penalties in this world. They also include sins carrying punishments in the Hereafter—that is, specific threats of punishment—such as sins that incur Allah’s wrath and curse, or Hell, or exclusion from Paradise. Examples include sorcery, deliberately swearing a false oath, fleeing the battlefield, mistreating one’s parents, giving false testimony, drinking wine, and similar acts. This is what has been reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other scholars.

Allah Most High says:

“If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will expiate your lesser sins and admit you to a place of honour.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Those who

avoid major sins and shameful deeds, except for minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And those who avoid major sins and shameful deeds, and who forgive when they are angry.”

And Allah Most High says:

“They will say, ‘Woe to us! What is this record that leaves nothing, small or great, without counting it?’”

And Allah Most High says:

“Everything, small or great, is written down.”

The gravest of the major sins is associating partners with Allah, followed by unlawful killing, then unlawful sexual intercourse. As Allah Most High says:

“And those who do not invoke another god besides Allah, nor kill a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed except with right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse”—to the end of the verse.

Unlawful sexual intercourse is graver than drinking wine when the two are comparable in extent—for example, committing unlawful sexual intercourse once and drinking wine once. But if we suppose that one man committed unlawful sexual intercourse once, while another habitually drinks wine, the latter’s sin may be graver than the former’s. Likewise, someone who committed unlawful sexual intercourse once and repented would be better than someone who persists in drinking wine.

Similarly, if a wine-drinker invites others to drink, he bears the sin of his own drinking as well as a share of the sin of those he invited. Likewise, when drinking is accompanied by listening to pipes, certain forbidden drinking practices, or the like, these aggravate the sin of drinking. A sin becomes more grievous through repetition, persistence, and the other sins accompanying it.

Likewise, if we suppose that someone committed unlawful sexual intercourse while fearing Allah and dreading His punishment, whereas the wine-drinker drinks heedlessly and frivolously, without being mindful of Allah, then the latter’s sin would be greater in this respect. Just as good deeds fall into categories of differing merit, yet a deed belonging to a lesser category may, in many circumstances, be better than one belonging to a superior category, so too it is with evil deeds.

Prayer is better than reciting the Quran, recitation is better than remembrance of Allah, and remembrance is better than supplication. Nevertheless, recitation, remembrance, and supplication after the dawn and afternoon prayers are better than deliberately choosing those times for voluntary prayer. Likewise, glorifying Allah while bowing and prostrating is better than reciting the Quran in those positions. Some people may benefit more from remembrance and supplication than from recitation, making these better for them.

The same applies to evil deeds. Although unlawful killing is graver than unlawful sexual intercourse, and unlawful sexual intercourse is graver than drinking wine, drinking may be accompanied by aggravating factors that make it more grievous than some of the harm caused by unlawful sexual intercourse.

Once it is understood that good and evil deeds differ in degree sometimes because of their categories, and sometimes because of other circumstances attending them, it becomes clear that one deed may outweigh another, and vice versa. A servant may perform a good deed with such intention, truthfulness, and sincerity that it outweighs many such deeds.

This is illustrated by the hadith of the man whose card, bearing the words “There is no god worthy of worship except Allah,” outweighed the scrolls containing his sins. Likewise, there is the hadith of the prostitute who gave a dog water using her leather sock, and Allah forgave her. The same principle applies to evil deeds. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
The Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About a man who habitually commits forbidden acts but regularly observes the five daily prayers, sends blessings upon Muhammad one hundred times each day, and says one hundred times each day, “Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, and there is no god worthy of worship except Allah”: will those sins be expiated through prayer and seeking forgiveness?

He replied:

Allah Most High says:

“Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

Whoever is a believer and performs a righteous deed for the sake of Allah Most High will not be wronged by Allah. Rather, He will reward him for it. As for the minor unlawful acts he commits, he deserves punishment for them, yet there is hope that Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. As Allah Most High says:

“And others have acknowledged their sins. They have mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil. Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness.”

If he dies without repenting, his affair rests with Allah, who knows best the measure of his good and evil deeds. We do not testify that he will enter either Paradise or Hell. This is contrary to the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah, who say that whoever commits a major sin has all his good deeds nullified.

Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah do not hold that good deeds are nullified in this way. Rather, those who commit major sins have both good and evil deeds, and their affair rests with Allah Most High.

translated_text:
As for the words of Allah Most High:

“Allah accepts only from the God-fearing,”

this means those who fear Him in that particular deed: it must be righteous, performed sincerely for the sake of Allah Most High, and in accordance with the Sunnah. As Allah Most High says:

“So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.”

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to say in his supplication:

“O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your sake alone, and let no one else have any share in them.”

The proponents of the doctrine of divine threats say that deeds are accepted only from those who fear Him by abandoning all major sins. This contradicts what the Quran and Sunnah teach, as in “the account of Himār, who used to drink wine, yet of whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said that he loved Allah and His Messenger.” It also contradicts the hadiths concerning intercession and the deliverance of those who commit major sins from the Fire, until even those with an atom’s weight of faith in their hearts are brought out of it. Allah Most High says:

“Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s permission,” and so on in the verse.

Nevertheless, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery; the thief is not a believer while stealing; and the one who drinks wine is not a believer while drinking it.”

He also said:

“Whoever drinks wine in this world and does not repent of it will be deprived of it in the Hereafter.”

And he said:

“Allah has cursed wine, the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, its seller, its buyer, its carrier, the one to whom it is carried, its drinker, the one who serves it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Section

Whoever repents of any sin whatsoever, Allah accepts his repentance, as He Most High says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. He is indeed the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.’”

“And return to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you; then you will not be helped.”

“And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly, while you are unaware.”

In this verse, Allah declares that He forgives sins—that is, for those who repent. In another verse, He says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

This concerns those who have not repented. Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, whereas anything less than that rests with Allah: if He wills, He punishes it, and if He wills, He pardons it. One form of associating partners with Allah is for a servant to call upon someone other than Allah, such as one who seeks deliverance in times of fear

This is among the forms of associating partners with Allah that Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, by the consensus of the Muslims.

The image of the shaykh whom one of these polytheists has called upon may appear before him. He supposes that it is the shaykh himself, or an angel who has come in his likeness. In reality, it is a devil that has assumed this form to mislead him and lead him astray because he called upon someone other than Allah. Such was also the lot of the idol-worshipping polytheists: devils would speak to them, appear before them, and tell them certain hidden matters, although the lies in what they reported made it clear that they were devils.

Allah Most High says:

“Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?”

“They descend upon every sinful liar.”

Such people are numerous among Indian, Turkic, and Abyssinian polytheists, and among the misguided people who profess Islam and imitate them. These include those who perform wondrous feats involving blood, saffron, and ladanum, claiming that they transform earth or other materials into such substances. Some enter fire and eat snakes; others shout at someone, causing him to fall ill or die.

who do not belong to the eight categories; by the consensus of the Muslims, it is not permissible to give these people zakat.

If these people say to someone, “Give to us, or I will inflict harm on you,” devils may indeed help them harm some people by Allah’s decree and predestination. But this happens to those who depart from the law brought by Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), such as people of immorality and religious innovation who do not perform the five daily prayers or regard as forbidden what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden. Some of these people have gained power over them because of their sins and misdeeds.

As for those who carry out what Allah and His Messenger have commanded, including the five daily prayers and other duties, and devote their religion sincerely to Allah—calling upon Allah alone, worshipping none besides Him, making vows only to Allah, and regarding as forbidden what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden—they are Allah’s victorious host and His successful party, for He strengthens them and grants them victory.

These believers defeat the devils of those misguided people. When these believers are present and seek Allah’s help, those people cannot manifest any of those satanic states; rather, those devils flee from the believers. These people themselves acknowledge this, saying:

“Our states have no effect in the presence of those who adhere to the Book and Sunnah. They take effect only in the presence of those who are not like them, whether Bedouins, Turks, ordinary people, or others.”

These are people of misguidance and error who must be forbidden from such conduct, called upon to repent, prevented from obeying Satan and from polytheism, religious innovation, and immorality, and commanded to do what

Allah and His Messenger have commanded, and to follow the Book and Sunnah. A believer must not fear them, for Allah Most High says in His Book:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

“So they returned with grace and bounty from Allah, untouched by harm. They pursued Allah’s pleasure, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.”

“It is only Satan who frightens you with his allies. So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.”

And He Most High says:

“So that people may have no argument against you, except those among them who do wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me, so that I may perfect My favour upon you and that you may be guided.”

“Just as We have sent among you a Messenger from yourselves, reciting Our verses to you, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know.”

“So remember Me; I will remember you. Be grateful to Me, and do not be ungrateful to Me.”

Repentance and seeking forgiveness concern both neglecting obligations and committing prohibited acts. Many people overlook the former.

Allah Most High says:

“So be patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true. Seek forgiveness for your sin, and glorify your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.”

And He Most High says:

“So know that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women.”

And He Most High says:

“So that Allah may forgive your past and future sins.”

“And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him; He will grant you good enjoyment for an appointed term.”

There are many such passages in the Quran.

We therefore say: Repentance and seeking forgiveness concern both neglecting a command and committing a prohibited act, for both are evil deeds, transgressions, and sins. Neglecting “faith,” “monotheism,” and the “obligations” Allah Most High has imposed upon the heart and body undoubtedly constitutes sin, as everyone acknowledges. Indeed, this is the graver of the two categories, as we have explained at length in what we wrote on “principles” before I went to Egypt. Neglecting obligations is, as a category, graver than committing prohibited acts, since it may include abandoning faith and monotheism. Whoever has faith and monotheism will not remain in the Fire forever, no matter what he may have done.

Whoever lacks faith and monotheism, however, will remain there forever, even if his sins involving actions are few. Such are the ascetics and devoted worshippers among the polytheists and the People of the Book, including the devoted worshippers among the polytheists of India, the Christian worshippers, and others. They do not kill, commit fornication, or wrong people, but they have neglected the very faith and monotheism required of them.

He replied:

“He did not mean this. Rather, he meant someone who introduces innovations into his religion or is wicked in his worldly affairs.”

I have discussed these “two types” at length elsewhere, as in our discussion in Iqtidā’ al-Sirāt al-Mustaqīm (Following the Straight Path) of Allah’s words:

“They enjoyed their share, and you have enjoyed your share just as those before you enjoyed theirs, and you have indulged in idle discourse as they did.”

A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere. Abandoning an obligation and committing a forbidden act necessarily go together. Hence, someone who does what he has been forbidden to do is said to have disobeyed the command.

If a man says to his wife, “If you disobey my command, you are divorced,” then forbids her to do something and she disobeys him, there are two views concerning this. The sounder view is that the divorce takes effect. Some jurists explain this on the grounds that such a person is considered disobedient in customary usage, while treating commands and prohibitions as fundamentally two distinct categories. The correct analysis, however, is that every prohibition contains a request and a demand for what the one issuing it intends. It is therefore a command, and the term “command” encompasses both.

An example is al-Khidr’s words to Moses:

“You will never be able to bear patiently with me. And how can you bear patiently with something beyond your knowledge?”

Moses said, “You will find me patient, if Allah wills, and I will not disobey any command of yours.”

He then told him:

“If you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.”

Thus his words:

“Do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you” is encompassed by his words:

“I will not disobey any command of yours.”

Another example is Moses’ statement to his brother:

“What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Have you then disobeyed my command?”

Moses had told him:

“Take my place among my people, put things right, and do not follow the way of those who spread corruption.”

This includes a prohibition. Moses rebuked him for not following him, saying, “Have you then disobeyed my command?” Those who worshipped the calf were spreading corruption, yet he described all of this as a command.

Likewise, Allah says:

“Angels, stern and strong, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded.”

Thus, they do not disobey Him when He forbids them something. He also says concerning the Messenger:

“Let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment afflict them.”

Anyone who commits what he has forbidden has therefore opposed his command. Allah Most High also says:

“Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray.”

Yet what he did was a forbidden act.

His words:

“It is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair”

apply even more strongly to what is forbidden than to what is commanded. For the Prophet said in an authentic hadith:

“When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Allah also says:

“On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were levelled over them.”

Disobedience means acting contrary to a command. Whoever violates a prohibition is disobedient, for he has acted contrary to a command. Someone who commits a forbidden act may be more clearly disobedient than someone who neglects a commanded act.

translated_text:
And, in sum, the two are inseparable. Whoever is commanded to do something is thereby forbidden to do its opposite, and whoever is forbidden to do something is thereby commanded to do its opposite, as explained at length elsewhere. However, the term “command” encompasses both categories. One of the two categories covered by a general term may be given a distinct name, while the general name remains in use for the other. Thus, “command” is a general term, but one of its two categories has been given the specific designation “prohibition.” When “prohibition” is mentioned alongside “command,” the latter refers to just one of the two categories, rather than encompassing both.

Section

The point is that seeking forgiveness and repentance concern both categories. One also seeks forgiveness and repents for what one did or left undone while ignorant, before knowing that such conduct was reprehensible and sinful, before a messenger was sent to one, and before the proof was established against one. For Allah, glorified be He, says:

“We never punish until We have sent a messenger.”

Some proponents of speculative theology and reasoned opinion have said that this applies to obligations established by revelation, not those established by reason. This view is held by some Muʿtazilites and others, including followers of Abū Hanīfah, and by others such as Abū al-Khattāb. Yet the verse is general: Allah does not punish anyone until He has sent a messenger.

translated_text:
Both contain evidence that He punishes only for sin, contrary to what is asserted by the “determinists,” the followers of Jahm: that He, exalted be He, punishes without sin. A group affiliated with the Sunnah, including al-Ashʿarī and others, followed him in this. It is also the view of Judge Abū Yaʿlā and others. They said that Allah may subject children in the Hereafter to endless punishment without their having committed any sin. They invoke this verse to refute those who say that reason requires the punishment of those who fail to act. Yet the verse is also evidence against them, since they allow punishment without sin. Thus, it is evidence against both groups.

There are similar verses in the Quran, such as His saying:

“Your Lord would never destroy towns until He had sent to their principal town a messenger reciting Our verses to them.”

And His saying, exalted be He:

“So that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

And His saying:

“Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’ They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error.”’”

What they did before the messengers came was sinful, reprehensible, and evil; however, the proof is not established against them until a messenger comes. This is the view of the majority.

It has also been said that an act becomes reprehensible only when it is prohibited. This is the view of those who recognize neither goodness nor reprehensibility except through commands and prohibitions. Such is the view of Jahm, al-Ashʿarī, and those who followed him among people affiliated with the Sunnah and among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad, such as Judge Abū Yaʿlā, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī, and others. One view is that their reprehensibility is known through reason, and that people deserve punishment for them in the Hereafter even if no messenger has come to them. This is maintained by the Muʿtazilah and many followers of Abū Hanīfah, who also attribute it to Abū Hanīfah himself. It is likewise the view of Abū al-Khattāb and others.

Another view is that, before divine instruction, such acts are neither reprehensible nor good nor evil. Rather, what is reprehensible is whatever one is told not to do, while what is good is whatever one is told to do or permitted to do. This is maintained by the Ashʿarīs and those who agree with them from the three groups.

A third view is that these acts are bad, evil, and reprehensible before the Messenger comes, but punishment is deserved only once the Messenger has come. This is the position of the generality of the early generations and most Muslims, and it is supported by the Quran and Sunnah. Both explain that the practices of the disbelievers are evil, reprehensible, and bad even before the messengers come, although they do not deserve punishment until a messenger has come.

It is related in al-Sahīh that Hudhayfah said:

“O Messenger of Allah, we were in a state of pre-Islamic ignorance and evil, then Allah brought us this good. Will there be any evil after this good?”

He replied, “Yes: callers at the gates of Hell. Whoever responds to their call to it, they will cast into it.”

Section

Allah Most High has described the reprehensibility of the disbelievers’ deeds before the messenger came to them, as in His words to Moses:

“Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. And say, ‘Would you be willing to purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord so that you may fear Him?’”

He also said:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing one group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was one of those who spread corruption. And We intended to bestow favor upon those who were oppressed in the land, to make them leaders, to make them inheritors, and to establish them in the land.”

This describes his condition before Moses was born and while he was still a child, before he brought Pharaoh a message: Pharaoh was already a tyrant who spread corruption.

Allah Most High also said:

“And We had already bestowed favor upon you once before, when We inspired your mother with what We inspired: ‘Place him in the chest and cast it into the river. Then let the river cast him onto the bank, where an enemy of Mine and his will take him.’”

That was Pharaoh. Thus, he was already an enemy of Allah at that time, although the message had not yet reached him.

Section

Furthermore, Allah commanded people to repent and seek forgiveness for what they had done. Had those deeds been like permissible acts, whose performance and omission are equally acceptable, or like acts that are pardoned, or the acts of children and the insane, they would not have been commanded to seek forgiveness and repent. This establishes that those deeds were reprehensible sins. Yet Allah does not punish until He has established the proof against people. Thus, Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware: worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am a warner and a bearer of good tidings to you from Him. Seek your Lord’s forgiveness and then repent to Him; He will grant you good enjoyment for an appointed term and give everyone of merit their due reward. But if you turn away, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous Day.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is One God, so turn steadfastly to Him and seek His forgiveness.’ And woe to those who associate partners with Him, who do not give zakah.”

He also says:

“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people: ‘Warn your people before a painful punishment comes upon them.’ He said, ‘O my people, I am truly a clear warner to you: worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me. He will forgive you some of your sins.’”

This indicates that their deeds were sins even before he warned them.

And He says concerning Hūd:

“And to ʿĀd We sent their brother Hūd. He said, ‘O my people, worship Allah

; you have no god other than Him. You are nothing but fabricators.’”

“O my people, I ask you for no reward for this. My reward rests only with Him who created me. Will you not then use reason?”

“And O my people, seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him.”

Thus, in his very first address, he declared them fabricators with regard to most of what they practised, just as he said to them in the other verse:

“Do you dispute with me concerning names that you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? Then wait; I too am waiting with you.”

Likewise, Sālih said:

“O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. He brought you forth from the earth and settled you upon it. So seek His forgiveness, then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive.”

Likewise, Lot said to his people:

“Do you commit a shameful act that no one in the world has ever committed before you?”

This indicates that their practice was already shameful before he forbade it, contrary to those who say that it was neither shameful, nor reprehensible, nor evil until he forbade it. Hence he said to them:

“Do you indeed approach men, cut off the road, and commit evil in your gatherings?”

These words address people who know the reprehensible nature of what they are doing, but he warned them of punishment.

Likewise, Shuʿayb said:

“Give full measure and weight with justice, do not deprive people of what is rightfully theirs, and do not spread corruption in the land.”

He made clear that what they had done

was depriving people of what was rightfully theirs, and that they had been spreading corruption in the land before he forbade them. This is contrary to the claim of “the determinists” that their wrongdoing was evil only because he forbade it, and that before the prohibition it was like any other action, such as eating, drinking, and so forth. They say the same about everything else the messengers forbade, including associating partners with Allah, wrongdoing, and shameful deeds.

Likewise, concerning Abraham, Allah’s close friend, He said:

“Mention Abraham in the Book. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.”

“When he said to his father, ‘O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, nor benefits you in any way?’”

This rebukes him for his conduct before it was forbidden. He also said:

“And Abraham, when he said to his people, ‘Worship Allah and fear Him. That is better for you, if only you knew.’”

“You worship only idols besides Allah and fabricate falsehood.”

Thus, He stated that they were fabricating falsehood before it was forbidden.

Likewise, Allah’s close friend also said to his people:

“What do you worship?”

“Do you seek, in falsehood, gods besides Allah?”

“What, then, do you think of the Lord of all worlds?”

—up to His words—

“Do you worship what you carve,

when Allah created you and what you make?”

All of this makes clear the evil of their practices before he forbade them and before he denounced their conduct. Hence his question expressed condemnation:

“Do you worship what you carve,

when Allah created you and what you make?”

That is, He created what you carve. How, then, can you worship what you make with your own hands and forsake the Lord of all worlds?

translated_text:
Had the goodness of affirming Allah’s oneness and worshipping Allah Most High alone, without partner, and the evil of associating partners with Him not been objective realities knowable through reason, he would not have addressed them in these terms. They would have done nothing deserving blame; rather, their conduct would have been like their eating and drinking. It would have become evil only through being forbidden, and its evil would have meant merely that it was forbidden, not that there was anything inherently evil in it—as the determinists maintain.

Furthermore, in many places in the Quran, He demonstrates through rational arguments the evil of their associating partners with Him and their other practices, and sets forth examples for them. Thus, Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?’
They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Then will you not take heed?’”

And He says:

“Then will you not fear Him?”

And:

“How, then, are you deluded?”

This implies that their acknowledgment that Allah is the Creator requires them to cease worshipping those objects, and that worshipping them is an evil, blameworthy act. Yet these people suppose that associating partners with Allah means believing that there is another creator. This is false. Rather, associating partners with Allah means worshipping anything other than Him, even if the worshipper acknowledges that what he worships is created.

His assertion, “It is all for Allah,” is a fabricated lie (1), even if he says, “It is created.” There are many such passages in the Quran, such as His words:

“Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water for you from the sky, with which We caused gardens of beauty to grow? You could never have grown

translated_text:
their trees. Is there a god alongside Allah? Rather, they are a people who set up equals with Him.”

“Or who made the earth a stable dwelling place, placed rivers throughout it, set firm mountains upon it, and placed a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god alongside Allah?”

In passage after passage, He says, “Is there a god alongside Allah?” He thereby reproaches them for worshipping anyone other than Allah and taking others as gods, despite their acknowledgment that no god other than Allah did these things: He alone did them.

To take His words, “Is there a god alongside Allah?” as answering the question, “What god exists alongside Allah?” is mistaken. They do indeed set up gods alongside Allah and testify to that; however, they did not say that those gods had done these things. A question intended to elicit acknowledgment must concern something they acknowledge. They acknowledge that those gods did not do these things; they do not acknowledge that there is no god alongside Him. Allah Most High says:

“Do you really testify that there are other gods alongside Allah? Say, ‘I do not testify to that.’ Say, ‘He is but One God, and I am free of whatever you associate with Him.’”

He, glory be to Him, also says:

“When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say, ‘Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself: whoever among you does evil in ignorance, then repents afterwards and makes amends—He is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”

And He says:

“The repentance Allah has pledged to accept is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterwards. It is they whose repentance Allah accepts.”

And He says:

“Then surely your Lord, to those who do evil in ignorance and afterwards repent and make amends, is thereafter All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Thus, although the Companions and the Successors said that every sinner is ignorant—as explained at length elsewhere—these words also encompass someone who knew that the act was forbidden. This shows that a person may be doing evil even without having heard the message clarifying what is forbidden, and that he may repent of it, whereupon Allah forgives him and has mercy on him, even though he does not deserve punishment until the message has reached him and the proof has been established against him.

Since repentance and seeking forgiveness may concern neglected obligations, as well as acts one did not know were sinful, it becomes clear how much falls within their scope. When repentance and seeking forgiveness are mentioned, many people think of reprehensible deeds they have committed and whose reprehensibility they knew through common knowledge, such as sexual immorality and manifest injustice. As for what is adopted as religion, only those who know it to be false recognize it as sinful. Examples include the religion of the polytheists and the altered religion of the People of the Book: these require repentance and seeking forgiveness, yet their adherents believe themselves to be rightly guided. The same applies to all religious innovations. Hence, a number of the early Muslim scholars—including al-Thawrī—said: “Innovation is dearer to Iblīs than sin, because people repent of sin but do not repent of innovation.”

This is the meaning of the statement reported from a number of them: “Allah has barred every adherent of innovation from repentance.” It means that he does not repent of it because he believes himself to be rightly guided. Were he to repent, Allah would accept his repentance, just as He accepts the repentance of a disbeliever.

As for the statement, “Allah has not permitted an adherent of innovation to repent,” its meaning is that, so long as he remains an adherent of innovation and regards it as good, he does not repent of it. But if Allah shows him that it is reprehensible, he repents of it, just as a disbeliever comes to recognize that he is misguided. Indeed, it is well known that many who followed an innovation came to recognize its misguidance, and Allah accepted their repentance from it. Only Allah can count their number.

When Ibn ‘Abbās was sent to the “Khawārij” and debated with them, half of them, or thereabouts, abandoned their position and repented. Others among them repented through ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz and others. Some heard religious knowledge being taught and repented; such cases are numerous.

This category of wrongdoing, whose perpetrators do not know it to be reprehensible, is widespread among those who face the qiblah in prayer, and is general among others. Likewise, the obligations a person neglects without knowing that they are obligatory are very numerous. Then, when he learns what good he had neglected—including affirming Allah’s oneness and having faith—and what sinful deeds he had been commanded to repent of and seek forgiveness for, the penitent repents of the duties owed to Allah Most High that he had neglected, squandered, or failed to fulfil, just as he repents of the evil deeds he committed.

Even if he committed those deeds and neglected those duties before the message reached him, it is through the message that he becomes deserving of punishment for those omissions and actions. Otherwise, as for his having committed blameworthy misdeeds and neglected good deeds whose omission is blameworthy, he had been repentant before that, as explained above. We have mentioned the “two views”: the view of those who deny both blame and punishment, and the view of those who affirm both blame and punishment.

translated_text:
If it is asked, “If a person is not punished for these deeds, what does it mean to call them reprehensible?” the answer is that their reprehensibility has two implications.

First, such conduct is a cause of punishment, but punishment depends on a condition: the establishment of proof. Allah Most High says:

“You were on the brink of a pit of Fire, and He saved you from it.”

Had He not saved them, they would have fallen. If someone standing at the edge perishes, his destruction depends on his falling, unlike someone who moves away from the edge and thus distances himself from destruction. Those who committed these deeds were therefore close to destruction and punishment.

Second, they are blameworthy, deficient, and flawed. Their rank is inevitably lowered by this. Even supposing they are not subjected to torment, they do not deserve the honour and reward that someone free of these faults deserves. This is punishment through deprivation of good, which is one of the two kinds of punishment. Although anyone who neglects a recommended act also misses out on its good, there is a difference between missing out on something one has not acquired and having what one already possesses diminished. This discussion applies generally to sins for which a person is not punished.

As for those to whom no messenger was sent in this world, reports have been transmitted stating that a messenger will be sent to them on the gathering grounds on the Day of Resurrection, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
People have differed over whether “obligation and prohibition” can truly exist without punishment for noncompliance, holding two views. Some say they cannot: if a person is not punished, the act is effectively permissible. Others say they can: the person must still be blameworthy, even if he is not punished. The truth of the matter is that punishment is of “two kinds”: punishment through suffering, which may be waived because of abundant good deeds; and punishment through a reduction in rank and deprivation of what one would otherwise have deserved. The latter occurs when the former does not.

Allah Most High expiates the sins of the wrongdoer, as He says:

“If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will absolve you of your lesser sins and admit you to a place of honour.”

Sometimes He expiates them through afflictions, so that the person’s rank remains as it was, or may even rise. He also expiates them through acts of obedience, but someone who did not commit those sins holds a higher rank. The sinner is thus deprived of the reward for the acts of obedience offset against his sins. This, too, is something of which a person who wishes to avoid loss repents. Someone who has neglected recommended acts also repents, so that he may obtain the reward they entail. Repentance therefore encompasses all these people.

A person’s repentance concerning his good deeds takes several forms. First, he repents and seeks forgiveness for his shortcomings in performing them. Second, he repents of deeds he thought were good but which were not, as is the case with the people of religious innovation. Third, he repents of his self-admiration and his view that he himself performed those deeds and that they were accomplished

by his own strength, forgetting Allah’s grace and kindness and that He is the One who enabled him to perform them. This is repentance from a blameworthy act and from neglecting what is commanded.

Hence it has been said: “Purifying deeds of what corrupts them is harder for those who perform them than prolonged striving.” This illustrates people’s constant need for repentance.

It has therefore been said: “Repentance is a station that the servant maintains from the moment he first enters it until the end of his life, and it is indispensable for all of creation.” Everyone must repent and persist in repentance.

Allah Most High says:

“Yet man undertook it. He was indeed unjust and ignorant.”

“So that Allah may punish the hypocrites, men and women, and the polytheists, men and women, and accept the repentance of the believers, men and women. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Thus, the ultimate aim of every believer is repentance.

Allah has said concerning the best of the prophets and the best of creation after the prophets—the earliest forerunners in faith:

“Allah has certainly accepted the repentance of the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had almost swerved. Then He accepted their repentance. Indeed, He is Most Kind and Most Merciful to them.”

Among the last revelations Allah sent down were His words:

“When Allah’s help comes and the victory,

and you see people entering Allah’s religion in crowds,

then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that “while bowing and prostrating, he would say, ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me,’ thereby putting the Quran into practice.”

" سُورَةَ الْمُزَّمِّلِ "
 وَفِيهَا قِيَامُ اللَّيْلِ بِقَوْلِهِ: {وَاسْتَغْفِرُوا
translated_text:
say before his death, ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.’”

She said: “I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I notice that you frequently say: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.”’

He replied: ‘My Lord informed me that I would see a sign among my community. When I see it, I will frequently say: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.” I have now seen it:

“When Allah’s help comes and the victory”—the conquest of Mecca—“and you see people entering Allah’s religion in crowds, then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”’”

His command—glory be to Him—that the Prophet glorify Him with praise and seek His forgiveness in these circumstances does not imply that this is not prescribed in other circumstances, or that others are not commanded to do so. Rather, it means that these circumstances are a reason for what he was commanded to do, even though he was also commanded to do it on other occasions. Likewise, a person is commanded to praise Allah and give thanks for His blessings, even though he is already commanded to give thanks for them; and he is commanded to repent of a particular sin, even though he is also commanded to repent of other sins.

Rather, this is a command that he conclude his deeds in this way. Others therefore have an even greater need for this than he did. A servant may also need this in other circumstances, just as he needs repentance. Thus, he needs repentance and seeking forgiveness at all times, as it is established in the Sahīh collection that “the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) would seek forgiveness three times after prayer.”

Allah Most High says:

“And those who seek forgiveness before dawn.”

They spent the night in prayer, then sat before dawn seeking forgiveness. Allah concluded Sūrat al-Muzzammil, which speaks of night prayer, with His words: “And seek forgiveness

from Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.” Likewise, He concluded Sūrat al-Muddaththir with His words:

“He is worthy of being feared and worthy of granting forgiveness.”

He—glory be to Him—is the One worthy of being feared. He did not say ahl li-l-taqwā, but rather “ahl al-taqwā” (“the One worthy of being feared”). He alone deserves to be feared and thus worshipped to the exclusion of all others. No one else deserves to be feared, as He says:

“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him belongs unceasing obedience. Will you then fear anyone other than Allah?”

He also says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah and is mindful of Him—it is they who will triumph.”

He is worthy of granting forgiveness, and no one else forgives sins, as Allah Most High says:

“And who forgives sins except Allah?”

In more than one hadith, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) says:

“Indeed, no one forgives sins except You.”

Thus He—glory be to Him—is worthy of being feared and worthy of granting forgiveness. Allah has linked affirming His oneness with seeking forgiveness in more than one passage, as in His words—glory be to Him:

“So know that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and women.”

Believers therefore seek forgiveness for having neglected to affirm Allah’s oneness and worship Him before embracing Islam, even if no messenger had yet brought them this, as explained previously. The Messenger likewise seeks forgiveness for what he had left undone, as Allah said of him:

“You did not know what the Scripture was, nor what faith was.”

This is so even though he was not liable to punishment for that. When a believer realizes that he has neglected the rights of his relatives or anyone else, he seeks Allah’s forgiveness for that and repents. The same applies when he realizes that some of what he does is blameworthy.
