Section

“Furthermore,” among the things for which one seeks forgiveness and repents are those thoughts within oneself for which one would be punished if one expressed them or acted upon them. Allah Most High says:

“Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.”

He forgives those who turn away from what is within themselves, neither expressing it nor acting upon it, like someone who intends an evil deed but does not commit it. If he refrains from it for Allah’s sake, a good deed is recorded for him. This, too, is something for which one seeks forgiveness and repents. Seeking forgiveness and repentance apply to everything that is a cause of blame and punishment, even if neither punishment nor blame has actually occurred, for it may lead to them. One therefore repents of it—that is, turns away from it—so that it does not lead to evil, and seeks Allah’s forgiveness for it—that is, asks Him to forgive him so that He does not make him suffer on its account. For even if he is not punished for it, it may nevertheless diminish him.

Although no evil deed is recorded against someone who entertains intentions of evil deeds, his preoccupation with them has distracted him from what would benefit him. He therefore falls short of someone who does not do so, but instead occupies himself with what benefits him.

We have explained at length elsewhere that a person’s deeds and words count either in his favour or against him; they necessarily fall into one of these two categories. Thus he seeks Allah’s forgiveness and repents for whatever

counts against him. He may also entertain false, evil suspicions, even without voicing them. When their falsity becomes clear to him, he seeks Allah’s forgiveness and repents. A person wrongs himself by neglecting an obligation just as he does by committing something forbidden.

Thus, in the words of Allah Most High:

“Whoever does evil or wrongs himself,”

the general category is mentioned after the particular. The same applies to His words:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins—and who forgives sins except Allah?—and do not knowingly persist in what they have done.”

Concerning His words, “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves,” some have said that indecency means unlawful sexual intercourse, while others have said that it means any major sin. As for the wronging of oneself mentioned alongside it, some have said that it too is an indecency, while others have said that it refers to minor sins. This accords with the view that indecency means a major sin, so that the passage encompasses both major and minor sins.

Those who say that indecency means unlawful sexual intercourse hold that wronging oneself includes all other forbidden acts. Another view is that indecency means unlawful sexual intercourse, while wronging oneself refers to acts short of it, such as touching, kissing and embracing. Others say that these acts constitute the indecency, while wronging oneself refers to sins. Yet another view is that indecency refers to deeds, while wronging oneself refers to words.

The correct understanding is that “wronging oneself” is a general category encompassing every sin. In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that Abū Bakr said, “O Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to recite in my prayer.” He replied:

“Say: ‘O Allah, I have greatly wronged myself, and none forgives sins but You. Grant me forgiveness from Yourself and have mercy on me. Indeed, You are the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”

And in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say in his opening supplication:

“O Allah, You are my Lord and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and acknowledged my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You. Guide me to the best character, for none guides to it but You. Turn bad character away from me, for none turns it away from me but You.”

The father of humankind and his wife said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.”

Moses said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.”

The Man of the Fish, Jonah, said:

“There is no deity except You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.”

Bilqīs said:

“My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with him—reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (1).

Allah has also said concerning the people of the towns who were punished:

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.”

As for His words:

“Forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs,”

it has been said that sins here means minor sins, while excesses means major sins. The correct understanding, however, is that “sins” is a generic term, while “excess” means overstepping the bounds and going beyond moderation, as in the pairing of sinfulness and transgression. Thus, sins correspond to sinfulness
translated_footnote: (1) Thus in the original.

translated_text:
and excess corresponds to transgression, as in His words:

“Neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit,”

and to going beyond what is needed. Sins include following one’s desires without guidance from Allah. All of this is sinful, as when someone’s pleasure and anger are driven by personal interests: such a person follows his own desires. “Excess,” by contrast, is exemplified by someone who becomes angry for Allah’s sake but then inflicts punishment beyond what Allah commanded. The verse occurs in the context of fighting the polytheists and what befell the believers on the day of Uhud.

Allah spoke of those who came before them, saying:

“How many a prophet fought alongside many devoted followers! They did not lose heart because of what befell them in Allah’s cause, nor did they weaken or yield. And Allah loves those who are patient.”

It has been said that, according to the correct interpretation, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the one meant here. Although he was not killed in battle, many prophets were killed.

“They did not lose heart because of what befell them in Allah’s cause, nor did they weaken or yield. And Allah loves those who are patient.”

“Their only words were: ‘Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs,’”

to the end of the verse. Thus they combined patience with seeking forgiveness. This is what is commanded when calamities strike: to bear them patiently and seek forgiveness for the sins that caused them. In battle, a person often fights for something other than Allah’s sake, as when he fights to display his courage, out of partisan zeal, or to be seen by others.

All these are sins. Someone who fights for Allah’s sake may nevertheless exceed the bounds, killing those who do not deserve to be killed and punishing the disbelievers more severely than he was commanded. Allah Most High says:

“If anyone is killed unjustly, We have granted his heir authority, so let him not

exceed the bounds in killing, for he has been granted support.”

And He says:

“And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor miserly, but maintain a balance between the two.”

And He says:

“And eat and drink, but do not be excessive.”

Excess, then, means overstepping the bounds. This is the last of what I have written here. Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best. All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.

الِاسْتِغْفَارُ يُخْرِجُ الْعَبْدَ مِنْ الْفِعْلِ الْمَكْرُوهِ، إلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمَحْبُوبِ مِنْ الْعَمَلِ النَّاقِصِ إلَى الْعَمَلِ التَّامِّ وَيَرْفَعُ الْعَبْدَ مِنْ الْمَقَامِ الْأَدْنَى إلَى الْأَعْلَى مِنْهُ وَالْأَكْمَلِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْعَابِدَ لِلَّهِ وَالْعَارِفَ بِاَللَّهِ فِي كُلِّ يَوْمٍ بَلْ فِي كُلِّ سَاعَةٍ بَلْ فِي كُلِّ لَحْظَةٍ يَزْدَادُ عِلْمًا بِاَللَّهِ. وَبَصِيرَةً فِي دِينِهِ وَعُبُودِيَّتِهِ بِحَيْثُ يَجِدُ ذَلِكَ فِي طَعَامِهِ وَشَرَابِهِ وَنَوْمِهِ وَيَقَظَتِهِ وَقَوْلِهِ وَفِعْلِهِ وَيَرَى تَقْصِيرَهُ فِي حُضُورِ قَلْبِهِ فِي الْمَقَامَاتِ الْعَالِيَةِ وَإِعْطَائِهَا حَقَّهَا فَهُوَ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى الِاسْتِغْفَارِ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ وَأَطْرَافَ النَّهَارِ؛ بَلْ هُوَ مُضْطَرٌّ إلَيْهِ دَائِمًا فِي الْأَقْوَالِ وَالْأَحْوَالِ فِي الغوائب وَالْمَشَاهِدِ لِمَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْمَصَالِحِ وَجَلْبِ الْخَيْرَاتِ وَدَفْعِ الْمَضَرَّاتِ وَطَلَبِ الزِّيَادَةِ فِي الْقُوَّةِ فِي الْأَعْمَالِ الْقَلْبِيَّةِ وَالْبَدَنِيَّةِ الْيَقِينِيَّةِ الْإِيمَانِيَّةِ.
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَتْ:
 دَائِرَةُ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ بَيْنَ أَهْلِ التَّوْحِيدِ وَاقْتِرَانِهَا بِشَهَادَةِ أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِمْ إلَى آخِرِهِمْ وَمِنْ آخِرِهِمْ إلَى
translated_text:
And Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Seeking forgiveness leads the servant from deeds that are displeasing to Allah to those that are pleasing to Him, from deficient deeds to complete ones, and raises him from a lower station to one higher and more perfect. For whoever worships Allah and knows Him grows in knowledge of Allah and in insight into his religion and servitude to Him every day—indeed, every hour, even every moment. He experiences this in his eating and drinking, sleeping and waking, speech and actions. He recognizes his shortcomings in maintaining an attentive heart at the higher stations and giving those stations their due. Thus, he needs to seek forgiveness throughout the night and at the ends of the day. Indeed, he is always in dire need of it, in his words and states, in things unseen and witnessed, because of the benefits it brings: securing good, averting harm, and seeking greater strength in deeds of the heart and body grounded in certainty and faith.

It has been established that seeking forgiveness encompasses those who affirm Allah’s oneness and is coupled with the testimony that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, from the first of them to the last, and from the last of them to

أَوَّلِهِمْ وَمِنْ الْأَعْلَى إلَى الْأَدْنَى. وَشُمُولِ دَائِرَةِ التَّوْحِيدِ وَالِاسْتِغْفَارِ لِلْخَلْقِ كُلِّهِمْ وَهُمْ فِيهَا دَرَجَاتٌ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَلِكُلِّ عَامِلٍ مَقَامٌ مَعْلُومٌ. فَشَهَادَةُ أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ بِصِدْقِ وَيَقِينٍ تُذْهِبُ الشِّرْكَ كُلَّهُ دِقَّهُ وَجِلَّهُ خَطَأَهُ وَعَمْدَهُ أَوَّلَهُ وَآخِرَهُ؛ سِرَّهُ وَعَلَانِيَتَهُ وَتَأْتِي عَلَى جَمِيعِ صِفَاتِهِ وَخَفَايَاهُ وَدَقَائِقِهِ. وَالِاسْتِغْفَارُ يَمْحُو مَا بَقِيَ مِنْ عَثَرَاتِهِ وَيَمْحُو الذَّنْبَ الَّذِي هُوَ مِنْ شُعَبِ الشِّرْكِ فَإِنَّ الذُّنُوبَ كُلَّهَا مِنْ شُعَبِ الشِّرْكِ.
 فَالتَّوْحِيدُ يُذْهِبُ أَصْلَ الشِّرْكِ وَالِاسْتِغْفَارُ يَمْحُو فُرُوعَهُ فَأَبْلَغُ الثَّنَاءِ قَوْلُ:
 لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَبْلَغُ الدُّعَاءِ قَوْلُ: أَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ. فَأَمَرَهُ بِالتَّوْحِيدِ وَالِاسْتِغْفَارِ لِنَفْسِهِ وَلِإِخْوَانِهِ مِنْ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ.
 وَقَالَ:
 إيَّاكَ وَالنَّظَرَ فِي كُتُبِ أَهْلِ الْفَلْسَفَةِ الَّذِينَ يَزْعُمُونَ فِيهَا أَنَّهُ كُلَّمَا قَوِيَ نُورُ الْحَقِّ وَبُرْهَانُهُ فِي الْقُلُوبِ خَفِيَ عَنْ الْمَعْرِفَةِ كَمَا يَبْهَرُ ضَوْءُ الشَّمْسِ عُيُونَ الْخَفَافِيشِ بِالنَّهَارِ. فَاحْذَرْ مِثْلَ هَؤُلَاءِ وَعَلَيْك بِصُحْبَةِ أَتْبَاعِ الرُّسُلِ الْمُؤَيَّدِينَ بِنُورِ الْهُدَى وَبَرَاهِينِ الْإِيمَانِ أَصْحَابِ الْبَصَائِرِ فِي الشُّبُهَاتِ وَالشَّهَوَاتِ الْفَارِقِينَ بَيْنَ الْوَارِدَاتِ الرَّحْمَانِيَّةِ والشيطانية الْعَالِمِينَ الْعَامِلِينَ 
{أُولَئِكَ حِزْبُ اللَّهِ أَلَا إنَّ حِزْبَ اللَّهِ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ}
 .
translated_text:
the first of them, and from the highest to the lowest. Affirming Allah’s oneness and seeking forgiveness encompass all creation, though people occupy different ranks before Allah, and everyone who acts has an appointed station. Bearing witness with sincerity and certainty that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah eradicates all shirk—associating partners with Allah—small and great, inadvertent and deliberate, first and last, hidden and manifest. It eliminates all its forms, subtleties, and concealed aspects. Seeking forgiveness wipes away one’s remaining lapses and erases sin, which is a branch of shirk, for all sins are branches of shirk.

Affirming Allah’s oneness thus removes the root of shirk, while seeking forgiveness erases its branches. The highest praise is to say, “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,” and the greatest supplication is to say, “I seek Allah’s forgiveness.” Thus, He commanded him to affirm His oneness and seek forgiveness for himself and his fellow believers.

He also said:

Beware of reading the books of the philosophers who claim therein that the stronger the light of truth and its proof grow within hearts, the more the truth eludes understanding, just as sunlight dazzles the eyes of bats during the day. Beware of such people. Instead, keep company with the followers of the messengers, who are strengthened by the light of guidance and the proofs of faith, who have insight concerning doubts and desires, who distinguish inward promptings from the Most Merciful from those of Satan, and who possess knowledge and act upon it:

“Those are the party of Allah. Indeed, it is the party of Allah who will be successful.”

وَقَالَ:

 فَمَنْ أَحَسَّ بِتَقْصِيرِ فِي قَوْلِهِ أَوْ عَمَلِهِ أَوْ حَالِهِ أَوْ رِزْقِهِ أَوْ تَقَلُّبِ قَلْبٍ:

{قَالَ حُذَيْفَةُ بْنُ الْيَمَانِ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إنَّ لِي لِسَانًا ذَرِبًا عَلَى أَهْلِي.
 فَقَالَ لَهُ:
 أَيْنَ أَنْتَ مِنْ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ؟ إنِّي لَأَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ فِي الْيَوْمِ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً}
 ".
translated_text:
He also said:

Repentance is among the greatest good deeds. All good deeds require sincerity to Allah and conformity to His command by following His Messenger. Seeking forgiveness is also among the greatest good deeds, and its door is wide open.

Whoever senses any deficiency in his speech, actions, condition, livelihood, or the changing states of his heart should turn to affirming Allah’s oneness and seeking forgiveness, for these bring healing when accompanied by truthfulness and sincerity. Likewise, if a servant finds himself falling short in fulfilling the rights of relatives, family, children, neighbors, and brethren, he should supplicate for them and seek forgiveness.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “I am sharp-tongued toward my family.” He replied, “What about seeking forgiveness? I seek Allah’s forgiveness more than seventy times a day.”

فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 بَلْ الْمُرَادُ الِاسْتِغْفَارُ بِالْقَلْبِ مَعَ اللِّسَانِ فَإِنَّ التَّائِبَ مِنْ الذَّنْبِ كَمَنْ لَا ذَنْبَ لَهُ كَمَا فِي الْحَدِيثِ الْآخَرِ:
 
{لَا كَبِيرَةَ مَعَ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ وَلَا صَغِيرَةَ مَعَ الْإِصْرَارِ}
 " فَإِذَا أَصَرَّ عَلَى الصَّغِيرَةِ صَارَتْ كَبِيرَةً وَإِذَا تَابَ مِنْهَا غُفِرَتْ.
 قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَالَّذِينَ إذَا فَعَلُوا فَاحِشَةً أَوْ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ ذَكَرُوا اللَّهَ فَاسْتَغْفَرُوا لِذُنُوبِهِمْ}
 الْآيَةَ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about the saying:

“One who seeks forgiveness is not persisting in sin, even if he returns to it seventy times in a day and a night.”

Does this mean merely uttering words of forgiveness, or must the person seeking forgiveness intend in his heart not to return to the sin? If someone repents of a sin, resolves in his heart not to return to it, and refrains from it for a time, but then commits it again, will the earlier sin be added to the later one, or will it have been forgiven through his earlier repentance? Will someone who repents of drinking wine and wearing silk drink wine and wear silk in the Hereafter? What are the conditions of sincere repentance?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah. Rather, what is meant is seeking forgiveness with the heart as well as the tongue. One who repents of sin is like one who has no sin, as stated in the other hadith:

“No sin remains major when forgiveness is sought, and no sin remains minor when one persists in it.”

If a person persists in a minor sin, it becomes a major sin; if he repents of it, it is forgiven. Allah Most High says:

“And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins”—and the rest of the verse.

{تَوْبَةً نَصُوحًا}

{مَنْ شَرِبَ الْخَمْرَ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَتُبْ مِنْهَا حُرِمَهَا}
 " وَقَدْ ذَهَبَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ كَبَعْضِ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد: إلَى أَنَّهُ لَا يَشْرَبُهَا مُطْلَقًا وَقَدْ أَخْطَئُوا الصَّوَابَ. الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ جُمْهُورُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ.
translated_text:
If his repentance is sound, his sins are forgiven. If he returns to the sin, he must repent again; and if he repents, Allah accepts his repentance again.

The scholars have differed concerning someone who repents of disbelief, then apostatizes after embracing Islam, and subsequently repents of his apostasy and embraces Islam again: are his earlier deeds restored? There are two views, depending on whether apostasy nullifies one’s deeds unconditionally or only if one dies in that state. The position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik is that it nullifies them unconditionally, whereas al-Shāfi‘ī’s position is that it nullifies them only if one dies in that state.

Apostasy is the opposite of repentance, and no sin other than apostasy erases all good deeds. Allah Most High says:

“Turn to Allah in sincere repentance.”

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—explained “sincere repentance” as repenting and then not returning to the sin. This is the complete repentance that is obligatory.

Whoever repents of drinking wine and wearing silk will wear the latter in the Hereafter, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever drinks wine and then does not repent of it will be deprived of it.”

Some people, including some of Ahmad’s followers, have held that he will never drink it under any circumstances. They have missed the correct view, which is held by the majority of Muslims.

عَنْ الْيَهُودِيِّ أَوْ النَّصْرَانِيِّ إذَا أَسْلَمَ، هَلْ يَبْقَى عَلَيْهِ ذَنْبٌ بَعْدَ الْإِسْلَامِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا أَسْلَمَ بَاطِنًا وَظَاهِرًا غُفِرَ لَهُ الْكُفْرُ الَّذِي تَابَ مِنْهُ بِالْإِسْلَامِ بِلَا نِزَاعٍ وَأَمَّا الذُّنُوبُ الَّتِي لَمْ يَتُبْ مِنْهَا مِثْلُ:
 أَنْ يَكُنْ مُصِرًّا عَلَى ذَنْبٍ أَوْ ظُلْمٍ أَوْ فَاحِشَةٍ وَلَمْ يَتُبْ مِنْهَا بِالْإِسْلَامِ.
 فَقَدْ قَالَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ:
 إنَّهُ يُغْفَرُ لَهُ بِالْإِسْلَامِ.
 وَالصَّحِيحُ:
 أَنَّهُ إنَّمَا يُغْفَرُ لَهُ مَا تَابَ مِنْهُ.
 كَمَا ثَبَتَ فِي الصحيح عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قِيلَ:
 
{أَنُؤَاخَذُ بِمَا عَمِلْنَا فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 مَنْ أَحْسَنَ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ لَمْ يُؤَاخَذْ بِمَا عَمِلَ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ. وَمَنْ أَسَاءَ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ أُخِذَ بِالْأَوَّلِ وَالْآخَرِ}
 وَ 
" حُسْنُ الْإِسْلَامِ "
 أَنْ يَلْتَزِمَ فِعْلَ مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَتَرْكَ مَا نُهِيَ عَنْهُ. وَهَذَا مَعْنَى التَّوْبَةِ الْعَامَّةِ فَمَنْ أَسْلَمَ هَذَا الْإِسْلَامَ غُفِرَتْ ذُنُوبُهُ كُلُّهَا. وَهَكَذَا كَانَ إسْلَامُ السَّابِقِينَ الْأَوَّلِينَ مِنْ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ وَاَلَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُمْ بِإِحْسَانِ؛ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ
translated_text:
He was asked:

If a Jew or a Christian embraces Islam, do any sins remain chargeable to him after embracing Islam?

He replied:

If he embraces Islam inwardly and outwardly, the disbelief of which he has repented by embracing Islam is forgiven, without dispute. As for sins of which he has not repented—for example, if he persists in a sin, wrongdoing, or an indecent act without repenting of it upon embracing Islam—some people have said that these are forgiven through embracing Islam. The correct view, however, is that only those sins of which he has repented are forgiven.

As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was asked:

“Will we be held accountable for what we did in the days of pre-Islamic ignorance?”

He replied:

“Whoever practises Islam well will not be held accountable for what he did in the days of pre-Islamic ignorance. But whoever does evil after embracing Islam will be held accountable for both his earlier and his later deeds.”

“Practising Islam well” means committing oneself to doing what Allah has commanded and abandoning what He has forbidden. This is the meaning of comprehensive repentance. Whoever embraces Islam in this manner has all his sins forgiven. Such was the Islam of the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness. For this reason, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said in the hadith

original_footnote: آخِرُ الْمُجَلَّدِ الْحَادِي عَشْرَ
translated_text:
which is authentic, to ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās:

“Do you not know that Islam wipes away what came before it?”

Here, the Arabic definite article refers to what was already understood, and the Islam understood among them was Islam practised well.

His words:

“But whoever does evil after embracing Islam will be held accountable for both his earlier and his later deeds”

mean that if he persists in the sins he used to commit, he will be held accountable for both his earlier and his later deeds. This is what the scriptural texts and justice entail: whoever repents of a sin is forgiven that sin, but it does not follow that his other sins must also be forgiven.

One who embraces Islam has repented of disbelief, as Allah Most High says:

“When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then let them go their way.”

And He says:

“Tell those who disbelieve that if they desist, their past will be forgiven.”

That is, if they desist from what they have been forbidden, their past will be forgiven. Ceasing to commit a sin is repentance from it. Whoever ceases to commit a sin is forgiven his past commission of it. But if someone does not cease to commit a particular sin, it does not follow that his past commission of it must be forgiven merely because he has ceased to commit another sin. And Allah knows best.
